general.temas: The war in Ukraine and its negotiations, the Russian economy, sport and culture recur across the front pages. Védomosti and Meduza report on an agreement between banks and telecom operators to identify bank calls. Meduza also highlights the detention of politician Yulia Galyamina in Kazan.
general.motivo_crispacion: The war pits Russia against Ukraine and confronts the United States and Europe with difficult negotiations and decisions about support. Rishi Sunak’s call to threaten Russian military facilities and a planned investigation by US senators into Starlink add to international tensions. In Russia, the detention of politician Yulia Galyamina and several cases of alleged corruption add to domestic conflict, although no protests are described. News about culture, sport, technology and business agreements partly offsets this atmosphere.

Kommersant.resumen:
- Preparations begin for the renovation of the Maxim Gorky House-Museum in Moscow.
- The convictions of former Russian Railways executives are upheld, and other cases involving alleged fraud and corruption move forward.
- The Finance Ministry proposes postponing the full application of the progressive tax scale to deposit income; a tax experiment involving staff recruitment is also being expanded.
- Russian companies are buying more servers, while confidence in opinion polls is declining.
- The front page covers visa restrictions on Russian athletes, Medvedev’s tournament, and developments in film and music.
Kommersant.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although the expression “visa war” introduces a confrontational note and some headlines use attention-grabbing wordplay.
Kommersant.sesgo: The selection focuses on Russian domestic affairs, particularly economic, judicial and institutional issues. The sports story presents visa restrictions from the perspective of Russian athletes.

Rossíiskaya Gazeta.resumen:
- The evacuation of a stalled Ferris wheel in Kazan continues; 18 people are reported to have been rescued.
- Sunak proposes threatening Russian bases in the Arctic; a Russian serviceman describes the use of drones against Ukrainian equipment.
- The Russian government supports the leasing of domestically produced helicopters, and changes to traffic rules are proposed.
- A concert will bring together songs by participants from different professions; a Werner Herzog documentary is also announced.
- The front page includes skating news and a striking story about a divorce in the United States.
Rossíiskaya Gazeta.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “superhero” and the headline about a divorce over a pig seek to grab attention.
Rossíiskaya Gazeta.sesgo: The selection gives space to Russian official initiatives and presents the conflict from the perspective of a Russian serviceman. It also highlights a British proposal to threaten Russian military facilities.

Komsomólskaya Pravda.resumen:
- The coverage is dominated by stories about Russian singers, their school memories, rumors and personal statements.
- Europe prepares for negotiations with Moscow over Ukraine, while Poland and Bulgaria limit their financial aid to Ukraine.
- One in six residents of Rome is reportedly on the brink of absolute poverty.
- Grigory Leps proposes studying the Bible in Russian schools and supporting conduct grades.
- Several celebrities describe how they celebrate their birthdays.
Komsomólskaya Pravda.motivo_populismo: Sensationalist or misleading headlines abound, such as presenting SHAMAN’s “addiction” to popular affection and saying that Stas Mikhailov “refuses to sing,” alongside phrases such as “Europe has its own plan.”
Komsomólskaya Pravda.sesgo: The front page prioritizes entertainment and Russian figures, while presenting Europe through economic problems, disagreements and doubts about its intentions. It also features a defense of Bible teaching from an Orthodox perspective.

Védomosti.resumen:
- Putin pardoned blogger Valeria Chekalina and expunged her criminal record.
- According to The Washington Post, a memo from Rubio to Trump led to Jensen Huang’s departure.
- Major Russian telecom operators and banks agreed to identify bank calls; Rosstat estimated quarterly GDP growth at 1% year on year.
- Rosatom expects to need up to 40 ice-class vessels over 10 to 15 years; Citilink filed another lawsuit against Wildberries.
- The front page includes analysis of sanctions on Russia, as well as reports and other content on history, technology and current affairs.
Védomosti.motivo_populismo: Informative headlines predominate, although expressions such as “harakiri for employees” and “the deal of the century” resort to sensationalism; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Védomosti.sesgo: The selection prioritizes Russian economic, business and institutional affairs, alongside attention-grabbing international news. No definitive political orientation can be discerned from these headlines.

Meduza.resumen:
- Media outlets publish alleged Kremlin demands for ending the war; Zelensky says the US proposed Ukraine’s entry into NATO in exchange for its withdrawal from the Donbas.
- Two Democratic senators ask Elon Musk to preserve documents concerning Starlink restrictions for Ukraine.
- Politician Yulia Galyamina is detained in Kazan; a former governor of Belgorod leaves his Telegram channel amid alleged Kremlin displeasure.
- Nearly $20 million is seized from a former Hungarian minister; major Russian banks agree to identify their calls.
- The front page includes cultural and historical news, advice on coping with the cold, the restoration of Microsoft services, and a maritime accident with no passenger casualties.
Meduza.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “maximalist demands” and “miracle on the Mississippi” add emphasis; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Meduza.sesgo: The selection prioritizes the war in Ukraine and Russian politics, with attention to the demands attributed to the Kremlin and the detention of a politician. The expression “maximalist demands” introduces a critical characterization of the Russian position.

opiniones.comunista:
Today I see a question of class behind apparently unrelated news stories: who controls the resources on which everyday life depends?

In Chita, the trial has begun of the co-owners of a company that supplies heat and electricity to Buryatia and Transbaikalia, who are accused of misappropriating funds. The presumption of innocence must be respected, but the case raises a political issue: essential services should not be subordinated to private profit. I advocate collective ownership, with transparent management and meaningful participation by workers and users.

At the same time, the Finance Ministry proposes giving banks another year to adapt their calculations for the progressive tax on deposit income. I understand the technical need, but postponing progressive taxation is also a decision about distribution. I prefer a system that asks more of those who have the most and finances decent public services for the entire working class.
opiniones.anarquista:
I am glad that Russia and Ukraine have resumed negotiations: stopping the war matters more than any state’s prestige. But I distrust a peace decided exclusively by governments and mediators who negotiate territories and alliances from above. Those who bear the consequences should have a real say in their future, not simply accept the agreement others sign.

I am also troubled by the detention of politician Yulia Galyamina in Kazan. The freedom to express oneself and organize cannot depend on permission from the authorities. I do not trust a different party to solve the problem on its own: every concentration of power calls for vigilance and resistance. I prefer to build mutual aid networks and autonomous assemblies, capable of making decisions from the bottom up and coordinating freely. Individual and collective freedom sustain each other; they are not granted from an office.
opiniones.liberal:
I worry that the tax debate is being reduced to postponing the application of the progressive scale to interest on deposits. I prefer low, simple taxes: saving is a responsible choice, and penalizing its returns leaves fewer resources in the hands of those who generated them.

I am also skeptical of the more than 2.4 billion rubles in public funds allocated to support helicopter leasing. Before choosing which industry deserves help, the state should ask whether taxpayers would not manage that money better themselves. A free market does not guarantee that every investment will succeed, but it does require those making the decisions to bear their own risks rather than pass them on to others. I want a limited state that protects rights and enforces the rules, not one that seeks to direct every economic decision.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see the same demand in the news: Russia needs sovereignty grounded in deeds, not rhetoric. Financing domestically produced helicopters is a step in the right direction: a vast country must retain its own industrial capacity and ensure connections with its most remote regions. I also take seriously the British proposal to threaten Russian facilities in the Arctic: national security cannot be left at the mercy of foreign political gestures.

But demanding strength abroad means demanding accountability at home. The conviction for abuses in the railways and declining confidence in polls should warn elites that patriotism is no substitute for accountability. And I welcome the debate over studying the Bible in schools: knowing the Orthodox tradition means understanding an essential part of our history.
opiniones.centro:
The resumption of talks between Russia and Ukraine is an opportunity we should not waste. But negotiating does not mean accepting just any agreement: I would support a peace that respects Ukrainian sovereignty and offers verifiable security guarantees. Consensus requires concessions, not one side imposing all its conditions.

I am also concerned about declining confidence in Russian opinion polls. Listening to society is of little use if people doubt the results or fear expressing their opinions. Trustworthy institutions need transparency and room for disagreement.

In the economy, slower growth calls for prudence, not resignation. I would support gradual reforms that encourage investment and competition, together with sustainable social protection. The market can drive prosperity; institutions must strive to ensure that its fruits are not reserved for a few.
